63: Moreover, Sariputra! The sentient beings born into that Land of Ultimate Bliss are all avivartika (non-retrogressive), and many among them are bodhisattvas of one-life-completing, whose number is so great that it cannot be known by calculation, but can only be spoken of as immeasurable, boundless, and innumerable.
64: -vartika] Sanskrit; rendered into Chinese as non-retrogressive. This means that after being born into the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one only advances stage by stage until Buddhahood, and never retrogresses. [One-life-completing] In this one lifetime one can fill the Buddha-position; this is an alternate name for the bodhisattva of the final body (the bodhisattva of equal enlightenment).

[Bodhisattva of equal enlightenment] The fifty-first among the fifty-two stages, the bodhisattva who is about to realize the Buddha-fruit; his merit and wisdom are nearly equal to the Buddha’s, and so he is called “of equal enlightenment.” For example, Avalokitesvara, Mahasthamaprapta, and Maitreya are all bodhisattvas of equal enlightenment. [Fifty-two stages] From an ordinary being to Buddhahood, a bodhisattva must pass through fifty-two stages: the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment. [Wondrous enlightenment] Enlightening oneself and enlightening others, with the practice of enlightenment completely fulfilled, and wisdom and virtue inconceivable, this is called “wondrous enlightenment”; it is the unexcelled right enlightenment of the Buddha-fruit, and one who realizes this right enlightenment is called a “Buddha.”
65: Question: When a sentient being is born into the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, he has no more birth and death, and becomes a Buddha in one lifetime. Why then does it say here that the bodhisattva of one-life-completing is one “who in this one lifetime can fill the Buddha-position”?
66: Answer: There are two kinds of birth and death: segmental birth and death, and transformational birth and death. When it is said that “a sentient being born into the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss has no more birth and death, and becomes a Buddha in one lifetime,” the one lifetime refers to one lifetime within segmental birth and death; while when it is said that “the bodhisattva of one-life-completing is one who in this one lifetime can fill the Buddha-position,” the one lifetime refers to one lifetime within transformational birth and death.
67: [Segmental birth and death] The sentient beings of the three realms and six destinies, because they are recompensed by good and evil karma, all have their lifespans limited and their bodies sectioned, and so their birth and death are called “segmental birth and death.” One who has ended segmental birth and death escapes the cycle and leaves the three realms. [Transformational birth and death] The sages of the three vehicles (the voice-hearer, the solitary-realizer, and the bodhisattva vehicles) have already cut off the delusions of views and thoughts and ended segmental birth and death. In the course of the Way, deluded thoughts gradually perish while realization gradually increases; this shift of delusion and realization differs from one period to the next. The passage from a previous period into a later one is exactly like a single birth and death, and its change is wondrous, subtle, and unfathomable, beyond thought, and so it is called “transformational birth and death.” One who has ended transformational birth and death fully realizes the Buddha-fruit.
68: [Sariputra! All who hear this should make the vow, “I wish to be born in that land.” Why is this so? Because then they will be able to associate with such excellent people, who all gather in the same place.]
69: Sariputra! When sentient beings hear of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, they should all make the vow, “I wish to be born in that land.” Why is this so? Because then they will be able to gather together with such a multitude of bodhisattvas of one-life-completing.
70: To be able to gather together with such a multitude of bodhisattvas of one-life-completing—what wonderful fellowship, and what unsurpassed conditions for study and practice is this
71: [Such excellent people] These are not merely good among human beings, but the good among the good, and so they are called excellent people. “Such excellent people” refers to the multitude of bodhisattvas of one-life-completing spoken of above.
73: [Sariputra! It is not by a small stock of virtue, merit, and karmic conditions that one can be born in that land.]
74: Sariputra! It is not by lacking the karmic condition of virtue and merit that one is born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
75: [Good roots] The good of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind; because they can produce wonderful fruits, they are called good roots. [The good of the three karmas of body (conduct), speech, and mind] Not to kill, not to steal, and not to commit sexual misconduct—this is good of body; not to speak falsely, not to speak divisively, not to speak harshly, and not to speak idly—this is good of speech; not to be greedy, not to be angry, and not to be deluded—this is good of mind. [Merit] The blessing recompensed by cultivating good conduct. [It is not by a small stock of virtue and merit, ’s karmic conditions that one can be born in that land.]
“It is not sentient beings of small good roots who shall be reborn in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitayus.”
[Sentient beings] Also called living beings, that is, all creatures endowed with consciousness.
76: In the Contemplation Sutra of Immeasurable Life, the Buddha says:
“Those who wish to be born in that land

should cultivate the three kinds of merit: first, to honor and support one’s parents, to serve one’s teachers and elders, to be compassionate and not kill, and to cultivate the ten wholesome deeds; second, to receive and uphold the three refuges, to fulfill all the precepts, and not to violate the dignified deportment; third, to arouse the bodhi-mind, deeply to believe in cause and effect, to recite the Mahayana, and to encourage those who practice.”
Therefore, those who recite the Buddha’s name must reverently cultivate the three meritorious practices of the Pure Land, so as to possess the karmic conditions of abundant virtue and merit.
77: [Ten wholesome deeds] The ten wholesome karmas: not to kill, not to steal, not to commit sexual misconduct, not to speak falsely, not to speak divisively (not to stir up quarrels), not to speak harshly (not to use cutting, abusive words), not to speak idly (not to speak meaningless words), not to be greedy, not to be angry, and not to be deluded (not to act contrary to right principle). See
An Explanation of the Ten Wholesome Karma Paths

. [Three refuges] The three refuges: taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, and taking refuge in the Sangha. This is taking refuge in the three jewels: the Buddhas are the Buddha-jewel, the right Dharma is the Dharma-jewel, and the noble sangha is the Sangha-jewel. [Arousing the bodhi-mind] Arousing the great mind that seeks the Buddha-way above (attaining Buddhahood) and saves sentient beings below.
78: The Buddha’s teaching of the three studies of precepts, concentration, and wisdom—the precepts are the foundation of concentration,
and those who recite the Buddha’s name should strictly uphold the five precepts and the ten wholesome deeds in order to increase their virtuous roots and merit

, and to lay a firm foundation. If one lacks virtuous roots and merit, one will constantly be deluded by the objects of the senses and entangled by karmic hindrances, and “the ten thoughts succeeding one another, accumulating habits until they become a second nature” will be hard to bring about. Therefore the Buddha, in the Amitabha Sutra, especially points out:
“It is not by a small stock of virtue, merit, and karmic conditions that one can be born in that land.”
In the Sutra of Immeasurable Life the Buddha says:
make your bodies upright and your conduct correct,
and further do many good deeds.
Cultivate yourselves and purify your bodies,
washing away the defilement of the mind.
Let words and actions be faithful and sincere, outward and inward in accord. If one can save oneself and then rescue and help others in turn, earnestly seeking the vow,
Though one toils for a single lifetime, in a brief moment, one will be born in the land of Immeasurable Life, with bliss unending.”
79: [Five precepts] Not to kill, not to steal, not to commit sexual misconduct, not to speak falsely, and not to drink intoxicants. Not to kill is not to take the life of a living creature; not to steal is not to take another’s property; not to commit sexual misconduct is to do nothing contrary to the marriage bond; not to speak falsely is not to tell deceitful lies; and not to drink intoxicants is not to consume drink or drugs that stupefy the mind.
80: Therefore, while earnestly reciting the Buddha’s name (the primary practice), one must also put an end to evil and do good (the auxiliary practice) in order to remove the obstacles on the path.

“Single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and at the same time cultivate worldly good as an auxiliary practice, following the method of Yongming and Lianchi, and there is nothing at which one will not succeed. One should reform one’s own evil and cultivate good, single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name. All one’s relatives, old friends, and those with whom one has karmic ties should also be taught in this way.”
(Reply to a letter from Resident Scholar of Yongjia, the sixth; he also said:)

“As for the method of practice, only the recitation of the Buddha’s name is the foremost, and therefore one should focus mainly on faith, vows, and recitation of the name. Then, adding ‘commit no evil, practice all that is good’ as an auxiliary practice, the benefit is great indeed.”
(Reply to a letter from Resident Scholar Fang Shengzhao, the sixth.)
81: [Doing good] To do charitable deeds is certainly doing good, but the most important doing good is still doing the good of one’s own three karmas of body, speech, and mind (

not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, not speaking divisively, not speaking harshly, not speaking idly, not being greedy, not being angry, not being deluded
). Therefore, doing good chiefly means doing the good of one’s own three karmas of body, speech, and mind. Master Shandao, an incarnation of Amitabha Buddha, set us a brilliant example:
“Guarding the precepts, not violating them in the least.”

(See the Record of the Sages of the Pure Land.) It is a pity that some doctrines nowadays broadly label the cutting off of evil and doing good as “mixed practice,” and set the conduct of the precepts in opposition to the recitation of the Buddha’s name, and even loudly proclaim that one need not cut off evil and do good, and that to do evil for a whole lifetime is of no account, because the evil person is the very object that Amitabha Buddha saves. (See
The Original-Vow Teaching Is a Teaching Mounted on the Buddha
.) [Conduct of precepts] The practice of guarding the precepts.
82: the Online Buddhist Academy of Renshuo Xixing’s

course schedule, the first stage is precisely “cutting off evil and doing good.” Through the study of this first stage’s courses one comes to understand the principle, the methods, and the practical steps of cutting off evil and doing good, and so can make the cutting off of evil and doing good more systematic, more thorough, and more solid.
83: At the same time, one should also cultivate the four immeasurable minds of kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, and apply them in daily life, to remove suffering and give joy, without resentment, without vexation, without anger, without hatred.
84: [Four immeasurable minds] The immeasurable mind of kindness, the immeasurable mind of compassion, the immeasurable mind of joy, and the immeasurable mind of equanimity. To give joy to all sentient beings is called the immeasurable mind of kindness; to remove the suffering of all sentient beings is called the immeasurable mind of compassion; to see others doing good, or freed from suffering and gaining joy, and to be filled with delight, is called the immeasurable mind of joy; and to let go of the above three minds without clinging to them, treating friend and foe alike, arousing neither affection nor aversion, is called the immeasurable mind of equanimity. Because these four minds universally connect with countless sentient beings and draw forth immeasurable merit, they are called the immeasurable minds.
85: Question: I too realize that cutting off evil and doing good is the foundation of Pure Land practice, but I find it hard to begin. What should I do?
86: Answer: On the question of where to begin in cutting off evil and doing good, I would especially recommend to you a short essay:
The Record of Yu Jingyi’s Encounter with the Kitchen-God (Original and Plain Speech)
The Notes on the Record of Yu Jingyi’s Encounter with the Kitchen-God

), which is a model example of reforming one’s destiny. I hope you will read it over and over, ponder it, grasp it, and put it into practice. Of these, the step of practice is especially important; only through continual practice can one realize the true meaning of the essay, and indeed the repeated reading, pondering, and grasping are all for the sake of practice. If time permits, it would be best to follow
the Online Buddhist Academy of Renshuo Xixing’s
course schedule, and to systematically study the five courses of the first stage, “cutting off evil and doing good.” Likewise, in this course of study the practical step remains the center.
87: It must be pointed out that the World-Honored One emphasized especially in the sutra:
“It is not sentient beings of small good roots who shall be reborn in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitayus.”

But the Original-Vow teaching loudly proclaims: to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss one “need not cut off evil and do good,” “need not uphold the precepts,” “doing evil and committing crimes is of no account,” “the evil person is the very object Amitabha Buddha saves,” “reciting the name one is certainly reborn,” “the gate of the great vow,” and so on (see
the essay “The Original-Vow Teaching Is a Teaching Mounted on the Buddha”

). This is nothing less than leading people toward a pit of fire, preaching in a manner directly opposed to the Buddha. The believers deluded by them neither earnestly recite the Buddha’s name (they were perfectly able to recite earnestly, but being deluded by them into thinking that “reciting the name one is certainly reborn,” they become careless and no longer recite earnestly), nor do they cut off evil, do good, and cultivate the ten wholesome deeds; indeed, some, emboldened (believing that “the evil person is the very object Amitabha saves”), recklessly do evil. The result is that not only are they not reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, but at death, drawn by their evil karma, they fall into the three evil destinies (hells, hungry ghosts, animals), unable to keep even a human body.
88: The function of cutting off evil, doing good, and upholding the precepts is: first, to tame the mind; second, to increase merit; third, to remove karmic hindrances. If one who recites the Buddha’s name neither cuts off evil and does good nor upholds the precepts, with a mind like a runaway horse or a mad elephant, how can he fix the mind in one place and attain the single-minded recollection without confusion? Merit is a help on the bodhi-way, while karmic hindrances are an obstacle. When merit (the help) is greater than karmic hindrances (the obstacle), what should be done, one is moved to do, and does it energetically and with enjoyment; what should not be done, one does not do, and can resolutely put down; at the end of life, the star of merit shines high, aiding rebirth. But when karmic hindrances (the obstacle) are greater than merit (the help), what should be done, one has no desire to do, and even if one forces oneself, one does it listlessly, doing little and stopping much; what should not be done, one does energetically and with enjoyment, tirelessly; and at the end of life, karmic hindrances appear and obstruct rebirth.
89: For example, knowing full well that “if the ten thoughts at the end of life succeed one another, one is reborn,” the foremost, most important matter for the reciter of the Buddha’s name is to recite the Buddha’s name at all times and in all places with ten thoughts succeeding one another, so that the habit becomes a second nature. Therefore, through all the hours of the day, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one should never let go of the ten succeeding thoughts; this is the great peace, the great liberation of the wise. Yet many who recite the Buddha’s name cannot do it. In truth, “through all the hours of the day, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, never letting go of the ten succeeding thoughts” is no harder than going to work, and being reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss surpasses becoming a billionaire by countless times! Why can they not “never let go of the ten succeeding thoughts,” yet for the sake of a little profit can suffer every grievance and toil day and night? The reason is that they are blocked by karma (analyze yourself, observe others, and you will understand how karma hinders). Therefore the Buddha here especially instructs:
“It is not by a small stock of virtue, merit, and karmic conditions that one can be born in that land.”
91: [Sariputra! If a good man or a good woman hears of Amitabha Buddha, and upholds his name, for one day, for two days, for three days, for four days, for five days, for six days, for seven days, with a single-minded mind unconfused; then when that person comes to the end of life, Amitabha Buddha, with the holy assembly, appears before him; and at that very moment, his mind undeluded, he is reborn in the Amitabha Buddha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss.]
92: Sariputra! If a good man or a good woman hears of Amitabha Buddha, and upholds his name, for one day, for two days, for three days, for four days, for five days, for six days, for seven days, attaining a single-minded mind unconfused; then when that person comes to the end of life, Amitabha Buddha, with the holy assembly, appears before him, in compassion and grace extends protection so that his mind is not confused, and he is reborn in the Amitabha Buddha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss.
93: [Good man] The Buddha calls a man who cultivates the five precepts and the ten wholesome deeds a good man. [Good woman] The Buddha calls a woman who cultivates the five precepts and the ten wholesome deeds a good woman. [Single-minded mind unconfused] The thought of reciting the Buddha is clear and distinct, neither dull nor scattered. As to what a single-minded mind unconfused is, Master Ouyi teaches:
is that the thought is clear and distinct, neither dull nor scattered.”
Occasional Talks in the Brahma Chamber.)
94: Regarding this passage of scripture, the eighth patriarch of the Pure Land school, Master Lianchi, teaches:

“This speaks of the recitation of the name. The Amitabha Sutra says: ‘When one hears of Amitabha Buddha and upholds his name, for one day, two days, up to seven days, with a single-minded mind unconfused. Then when that person comes to the end of life, Amitabha Buddha, with the holy assembly, appears before him. At that time his mind, unconfused, is reborn in the Amitabha Buddha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss.’ This is the recitation of the name for ten thousand ages
, and is personally proclaimed by the golden mouth
(The Collected Sayings of Yunqi on the Pure Land.)
95: Master Lianchi’s teaching here means: this passage on a single-minded mind unconfused is the fundamental basis (the great source from which it issues) for the recitation of the name for ten thousand ages, and is the wondrous Dharma of rebirth personally proclaimed by the golden mouth of the World-Honored One. Therefore, those who recite the Buddha’s name must strictly follow this passage in their practice, so as to ensure rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
96: As for what it is to correctly uphold the name,
the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, Master Chewu, teaches:
“That which is called upholding the name means to clasp it to one’s breast with firm devotion
, that is, to hold it fast in the mind and never for a moment forget it.
If there is the least interruption of a single thought
(the thought of recitation being interrupted by a wandering thought)
, then it is no longer upholding. If there is the least admixture of a single thought
(the least admixture of a wandering thought)
, then it is no longer upholding. When thought after thought succeeds without admixture or interruption, that is true diligence.
one gradually enters the single-minded mind unconfused
, and fully accomplishes the Pure Land practice.”
97: [Classp it to one’s breast with firm devotion (

)] “Classp it to one’s breast”: to hold firmly and not let go, extended to mean earnest; “firm devotion”: to bear it in mind fervently. “Clasp it to one’s breast with firm devotion” describes earnestly bearing in mind without forgetting.
98: Question: What are the single-mindedness in affairs and the single-mindedness in principle?
99: Answer: The single-mindedness in affairs and the single-mindedness in principle are also called the mind unconfused in affairs and the mind unconfused in principle. The recitation of the name has a holding in affairs and a holding in principle. The holding in affairs is to recite Amitabha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; the holding in principle is to recite the self-nature Buddha (the Amitabha of self-nature). The holding in affairs is urgent for rebirth; the holding in principle aims at seeing one’s nature.

The single-mindedness in affairs is that the thought is clear and distinct, neither dull nor scattered; the single-mindedness in principle is to accord quietly with the unborn, and to illumine clearly one’s self-nature.
Middle dot Occasional Talks in the Brahma Chamber.)
the essay “Single-Mindedness in Affairs and Single-Mindedness in Principle”
100: Question: Does the “clear and distinct” spoken of above mean that the Buddha-name should be recited very clearly?
101: Answer: That is not the meaning. “Clear and distinct” means this: the Buddha-name being recited should be clear and distinct in the mind (each sentence of the Buddha-name is clearly known in the mind).
102: Question: What does “neither dull nor scattered” mean?
103: Answer: “Neither dull nor scattered” means: neither dullness nor scatteredness. That is, if a wandering thought arises, know it and do not follow it, not be thrown into confusion by it. Therefore, the single-minded mind unconfused in recitation does not mean that not one wandering thought arises, but that one is not deluded by wandering thoughts, and does not let wandering thoughts succeed one another into a train of thought. In short, one is not thrown into confusion by wandering thoughts. Of course, this is only the most elementary requirement of a single-minded mind unconfused; making further effort upon this foundation, one will reach the realm where there is no wandering thought in thought after thought, and the Buddha-name is a single, pure field.
104: “For one day, for two days, for three days, for four days, for five days, for six days, for seven days, with a single-minded mind unconfused.”
Within a single day, even within seven days, can one truly attain a single-minded mind unconfused?
105: Answer: “For one day up to seven days” is an enumerative phrase, an abridged expression. The detailed expression, for example, is what the World-Honored One said in the Great Discourse on the Application of Mindfulness:
“Bhikkhus! Anyone who, in this way, rightly cultivates the four applications of mindfulness
, may expect one of two fruits: either the highest wisdom in this very life
, or, if the five aggregates still remain, the fruit of non-return
, if anyone, in this way, rightly cultivates the four applications of mindfulness
may expect one of two fruits: either the highest wisdom in this very life, or, if the five aggregates still remain, the fruit of non-return.”
106: [Four fruits] Cultivating the four noble truths has four fruits: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-return, and the fruit of arhatship. Among them, the fourth fruit, the arhat, is the highest; one who reaches this fruit is released from birth and death and receives no further becoming.
107: As for the question “within a single day, even within seven days, can one attain a single-minded mind unconfused,” the answer is: the single-minded mind unconfused in recitation is the realm of the ten thousand thoughts returning to the One, and the ten thousand thoughts returning to the One is only the most elementary realm of practice. For the Chan school, one must pass through the ten thousand thoughts returning to the One, and the One returning to nothing, and so clarify the mind and see one’s nature
, and then do the work of guarding, until the delusions of views and thoughts are entirely cut off, only then can one end birth and death and escape the cycle

. Therefore, some Chan practitioners have already had the ten thousand thoughts return to the One, but are still quite far from clarifying the mind and seeing their nature; once they hear of the supreme excellence of the Pure Land teaching and turn to recitation, they can attain a single-minded mind unconfused in recitation within a single day, even within seven days. Since ancient times such examples have been too numerous to list singly; see the Record of the Sages of the Pure Land. And Chan practitioners who have already clarified the mind and seen their nature, turning to cultivate the Pure Land teaching, can within a single day attain a single-minded mind unconfused in recitation, and many afterwards became masters and virtues of the Pure Land school; see the Record of the Sages of the Pure Land. For example, Master Chewu, who was the thirty-sixth patriarch of the Linji school, broadened the lecture platform and led the assembly in Chan, spurring on later students with tireless delight. Fourteen years as one day, his fame spread through the south and north, and the linage spirit was greatly revived. But later, whenever he recalled Master Yongming (the sixth Pure Land patriarch), a master of the Chan lineage, who nonetheless set his heart on the Pure Land and recited the Buddha’s name a hundred thousand times a day, longing to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; and how much more, in this age of the Dharma’s end, should one follow the legacy of Master Yongming. So he left the Chan monastery and practiced exclusively the Pure Land, teaching countless beings, and became the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school.
108: As for those who study the Buddha’s teaching who have not generally yet attained the returning of the ten thousand thoughts to the One, the time will be somewhat longer; how long it will take depends on each person’s foundation and progress. Generally speaking, as long as the method is correct (for example, cultivating according to

), through diligent effort everyone can attain the single-minded mind unconfused in recitation. This matter requires self-confidence (profound faith that one can attain the single-minded mind unconfused), constancy, and perseverance. That self-confidence, constancy, and perseverance can change one’s destiny, Yu Jingyi set us an excellent example; see
The Record of Yu Jingyi’s Encounter with the Kitchen-God (Original and Plain Speech)
The Notes on the Record of Yu Jingyi’s Encounter with the Kitchen-God
109: Therefore, those who recite the Buddha’s name must have true faith and sincere vows, and be diligent without respite. Though one toils for a lifetime, it is but a moment; and once one reaches the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one’s lifespan is immeasurable, bliss is unending, and one becomes a Buddha and saves sentient beings, fulfilling the great vow of bodhi.
110: Question: How does one attain a single-minded mind unconfused?
111: the essay “How to Attain a Single-Minded Mind Unconfused”
112: Question: The Praise of the Buddha’s Reception Sutra says:

“For one day and night, or two, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven, with the thought bound without confusion. When that good man or good woman comes to the end of life, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, together with his countless disciples and the assembly of bodhisattvas, surrounded front and back, comes and stands before him,
and in compassion and grace extends protection, so that his mind is not confused.
Having given up his life, he follows the Buddha’s assembly and is born in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Immeasurable Life.”

Since one has already attained the thought bound without confusion (the single-minded mind unconfused), why does it then speak of Amitabha’s coming and, after his coming, “in compassion and grace extending protection, so that his mind is not confused”?
113: Answer: The thought bound without confusion (the single-minded mind unconfused) is the cause that draws the Buddha to come welcome, but the thought bound without confusion is a shallow-level practice, often insufficient to maintain the mind unconfused at the moment when the four elements decompose, suffering presses in, and demons manifest. Therefore Amitabha’s “in compassion and grace extending protection, so that the mind is not confused” ensures rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The Sutra of Praising the Merit of the Buddhas says:
“When one’s life is about to end, with a single mind of faith and joy, the thought not forgotten and not abandoned
this is the right thought at the end of life, drawing the Buddha to come welcome
and stand before him; and the demons will at last be unable to destroy

Here, “the demons will at last be unable to destroy their mind of right enlightenment” is precisely because of Amitabha’s “in compassion and grace extending protection, so that the mind is not confused.”
114: [Sariputra! I see this benefit, and therefore speak these words. If there are sentient beings who hear these words, they should make the vow, “I wish to be born in that land.”]
115: Sariputra! I see such supreme benefit, and therefore speak these words (that upholding the name with a single-minded mind unconfused assures rebirth). If there are sentient beings who hear this message that upholding the name with a single-minded mind unconfused assures rebirth, they should make the vow, and cultivate as is taught, to be born in that land.
116: “Sariputra! I, observing such great matter of benefit and peace, speak these truthful words: if any pure-hearted good man or good woman, having heard of such inconceivable merit of the name of the Buddha Immeasurable Life, and of the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, should believe, accept, and make the vow,
he is born in that Buddha-land.”
117: [Therefore I speak these words] These words are:

“If a good man or a good woman hears of Amitabha Buddha, and upholds his name, for one day, for two days, for three days, for four days, for five days, for six days, for seven days, with a single-minded mind unconfused; then when that person comes to the end of life, Amitabha Buddha, with the holy assembly, appears before him; and at that very moment, his mind undeluded, he is reborn in the Amitabha Buddha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss.”
118: The vow here is made after the World-Honored One has told of the certain rebirth of one who upholds the name with a single-minded mind unconfused, and then immediately says: “I see this benefit, and therefore speak these words. If there are sentient beings who hear these words, they should make the vow, ‘I wish to be born in that land.’” Therefore, the vow here is the vow of “upholding the name with a single-minded mind unconfused,” so as to ensure rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
119: 5. The Buddhas of the Various Quarters Praise
120: [Sariputra! Just as I now praise the inconceivable virtue and benefit of Amitabha Buddha, so too in the east there are the Buddhas Akshobhya

Buddha, Sumeru-form Buddha, Great Sumeru Buddha, Sumeru-light Buddha, and Wondrous-sound Buddha; and such Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each in his own land puts forth the broad and long tongue, covering the whole three-thousand-great-thousand world, and speaks these truthful words: “You sentient beings shall believe in this sutra that praises inconceivable virtue and is protected and kept in mind by all the Buddhas.”]
121: Sariputra! Just as I now praise the inconceivable virtue and benefit of Amitabha Buddha, so too in the east there are Akshobhya Buddha, Sumeru-form Buddha, Great Sumeru Buddha, Sumeru-light Buddha, and Wondrous-sound Buddha, and such Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each in his own land puts forth the broad and long tongue, and speaks these truthful words to the entire three-thousand-great-thousand world he teaches: “You sentient beings should all believe and accept this sutra that praises the inconceivable virtue of Amitabha Buddha and is protected and kept in mind by all the Buddhas.”
